name: Pacific Northwest Rainforest
blurb: Giant conifers, mossy elk country and salmon that feed the forest from the sea.

tip.title: Empty the river of salmon
tip.text: Salmon carry ocean nutrients into the forest. Set Pacific salmon to -100% and watch the eagles, bears and the streamside trees.

sources.title: Helfield & Naiman 2001, Ecology: salmon-derived nitrogen and riparian forest growth

notes: Feeding links were checked against the sources listed where they state them. Where the sources are silent, links come from general ecological knowledge and are illustrative. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Gaps in the tall canopy let light reach the mosses, shrubs and seedlings below.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead wood, needles and salmon carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
A giant conifer of the wet coastal forest. Near spawning streams its foliage draws a share of its nitrogen from salmon carcasses.
One of the main canopy conifers of the Olympic rainforest, alongside spruce and Douglas-fir.
A tall canopy conifer; old stands of it provide the nesting habitat northern spotted owls need.

nodes.name: Krill and small ocean prey
nodes.desc: Small crustaceans that graze plankton and feed salmon and other fish at sea.
A large yellow forest slug that eats fungi, plant matter and litter, and helps spread seeds.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: Omnivore that eats berries, shoots and insects, and fishes for salmon in the Pacific coast; it also strips bark.
In the Pacific Northwest, spawning salmon make up most of its diet from late summer through fall, mostly scavenged carcasses.

nodes.name: Cougar
nodes.desc: The park's top land predator; deer and elk are the main prey of cougars, and it is among the predators of elk.

link_ideas.what: Salmon carry marine nitrogen from the ocean into forest streams
